sections.h2: Who records deeds in DuPage County, Illinois?
sections.html:
The DuPage County Recorder's Office takes in, reviews, records and keeps every deed, mortgage, lien and plat for property in the county. Its collection reaches back to 1839, the year DuPage was cut out of Cook County.

The office is fee funded, so recording charges pay for its operations. Its public line is 630-407-5400 and its research desk answers at 630-407-5401. The counter is open weekdays from 8 a.m. until half past four, and closed on county holidays. Closing companies commonly prepare the deed packet, pay the fees and submit it, so a seller mainly needs to know what gets charged and why.

sections.h2: What fee does the DuPage County Recorder set for a deed?
sections.html:
A standard deed carries an $86.00 filing fee in DuPage County. Nonstandard paper documents cost more, and plats have their own price.

DuPage County Recorder fee schedule for common documents (source: DuPage County Recorder forms and fee schedules)
DocumentRecording fee
Deed (Class 1)$86.00
Lease (Class 2)$86.00
Mortgage (Class 3)$86.00
Easement (Class 4)$86.00
Nonstandard document (Class 5)$112.00
Miscellaneous (Class 7)$86.00
Map or plat (Class 8)$110.00
Military discharge (DD214)No charge

The office states that each fee already includes a $10 document storage charge, a $31 geographic information system charge, a $1 real property charge and an $18 Rental Housing Support Program charge. Copies cost $0.50 a page and a certification costs $5.00 a document. Payment comes with the submission, and the office takes credit cards, checks, money orders and cash. Card payments add a convenience fee: $2.00 on charges of $59.99 or less, and 2.75% on $60.00 or more.

sections.h2: What goes into a DuPage County deed package?
sections.html:
You need a completed deed plus the transfer forms that go with it. The Recorder's Office cannot draft a deed or tell you what your particular document must say, so an attorney or title company handles that part.

The office lists these items for a deed package:

  • The signed deed itself
  • The PTAX form or an exemption statement
  • Municipal transfer stamps, where the village or city requires them
  • A metes and bounds affidavit, if one applies
  • The buyer's name and mailing address for the tax bill
  • The property address and the permanent parcel number from the tax bill
  • The legal description
  • The preparer's name and address

A document that is incomplete is returned to whoever sent it. A recorded deed is stamped with a number and date, indexed and imaged, then mailed back to the address given, or returned electronically when it came in through eRecording. To change only the name and mailing address on a tax bill, the office points owners to the County Clerk.

sections.h2: How does transfer tax work on a DuPage County sale?
sections.html:
Illinois charges a state transfer tax through revenue stamps sold at 50 cents for each $500 of value or fraction of $500, under 35 ILCS 200/31-15. The Recorder sells the stamps, and since paper stamps were phased out at the end of 2025, counties issue electronic stamps or similar proof of payment.

Each sale also needs a signed real estate transfer declaration, Form PTAX-203, with at least one seller and one buyer (or their agents) signing. The Illinois Department of Revenue handles questions about the form and the MyDec online tool at 844-445-1114. The DuPage Recorder has accepted MyDec-prepared forms since January 14, 2015.

Some deeds are exempt from the tax under 35 ILCS 200/31-45. The DuPage list includes deeds where the actual consideration is under $100, tax deeds, deeds that only correct or confirm an earlier recorded deed, deeds of partition, and deeds issued to a mortgage holder after foreclosure or in lieu of foreclosure. Deeds exempt under paragraphs (b), (k) or (m) of the county list still need a PTAX-203. The county references its own Resolution F11879 for local transfer rules, so ask the Recorder which stamps your deed needs.

sections.h2: Which DuPage municipalities charge their own transfer stamp?
sections.html:
Some do, and some do not. The Recorder publishes a list of municipal fees and tells owners to contact the village or city before closing, since the amounts can change without notice to the office.

  • Elmhurst: $1.50 per $1,000, exemption stamp $30.00
  • Addison: $2.50 per $1,000, exemption stamp $50.00
  • Wheaton: $2.50 per $1,000, exemption stamp $25.00
  • Woodridge: $2.50 per $1,000, exemption stamp $25.00
  • Naperville: $3.00 per $1,000, no exemption stamp charge
  • Glen Ellyn: $3.00 per $1,000, no exemption stamp charge
  • Carol Stream: $3.00 per $1,000, exemption stamp $25.00
  • Bolingbrook: $7.50 per $1,000, exemption stamp $50.00

The county page also lists Aurora, Bartlett, Elk Grove, Glendale Heights and Hanover Park. For a town missing from that list, ask the village or city hall whether a local stamp applies before closing.

sections.h2: Can I record a deed online in DuPage County?
sections.html:
Yes. The Recorder accepts deeds, mortgages, releases, liens and similar documents through electronic recording. Plats and DD-214 discharge forms are not accepted electronically.

Electronic recording runs through an account with an approved vendor. The county names Corporation Service Company, eRecording Partners Network, Hopdox, Indecomm Global Services and Simplifile. Any setup fee is a matter between the customer and the vendor. Most sellers never open such an account, because their closing company already has one.

The other routes are to hand the document in at the office or mail it to the office's mailing address. Documents recorded electronically come back electronically.

sections.h2: How far back do DuPage County property records go?
sections.html:
The office keeps records from 1839 to the present. Computer searches cover names from 1961, parcel numbers from 1985 and property addresses from 1995, and plats can be searched back to the 1800s.

Searching and printing images through the online search is free. A copy of a deed shows who owns the property but says nothing about liens, so it is not a substitute for a title search. The office states that it does not run full title searches and carries no errors and omissions coverage, so a title insurance company does that work. A copy of a satisfaction shows that a mortgage was paid off once it has been recorded.

sections.h2: What is DuPage County like for a home seller?
sections.html:
DuPage County sits west of Chicago and is one of the collar counties of the metro area. The Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 934,298 residents, and the county seat is Wheaton, with Naperville as the largest city. It touches Cook County to the east and north, Will County to the south, Kane County to the west and Kendall County at a corner.

QuickFacts reports 370,517 housing units, a 73.1% owner-occupied rate and a median value of $391,400 for owner-occupied homes in 2020 through 2024. Median household income for the same period is $112,096 and median gross rent is $1,688. The county covers 327.80 square miles of land and drew 1,265 building permits in 2025.

Employers include Oak Brook's Hub Group and Ace Hardware, Naperville's Nicor Gas, Lisle's Molex and the two national laboratories, Argonne in the southeast and Fermilab on the Kane County line. Oakbrook Center, Fox Valley Mall and Yorktown Center anchor the shopping.

sections.h2: How are property taxes handled around a DuPage County closing?
sections.html:
Property tax is billed in arrears, so a bill issued in 2026 covers the 2025 tax year. DuPage mails one bill with two payment coupons, and for 2025 taxes the installments were due June 1 and September 1, 2026, both of which have passed.

The Treasurer's Office, at 630-407-5900, collects the tax but does not set values, so questions about an assessment go to the assessor whose number is on the bill. The County Clerk calculates the tax on each parcel and certifies it to the Treasurer. Look for the exemptions listed on the bill, since the Treasurer reports that both the general homestead and senior exemptions are $8,000 each. If a mortgage company pays the bill, a yellow box on the bill says so, and a second payment would only create a refund request. The Treasurer reports just under $4 million in such duplicate payments in a recent year.

faqs.q: What is the DuPage County deed filing price?
faqs.a: The DuPage County Recorder charges $86.00 for a standard deed. That price includes storage, GIS, real property and rental housing support charges. A nonstandard document costs $112.00 and a plat $110.00. Card payments carry a convenience fee on top.

faqs.q: Does the DuPage County Recorder write or review my deed?
faqs.a: No. The office checks that a document meets recording requirements but cannot prepare a deed or give legal advice. Deed forms come from an attorney, a title company or a form seller, and an incomplete package is returned to the sender.

faqs.q: Do I pay Illinois transfer tax if I sell my DuPage County house?
faqs.a: Usually yes, because the state tax is collected through revenue stamps at 50 cents per $500 of value when the deed is recorded. Certain deeds are exempt under 35 ILCS 200/31-45, such as tax deeds and corrective deeds. Exempt deeds in some categories still need a PTAX-203.

faqs.q: Can I look up my deed online for free in DuPage County?
faqs.a: Yes. The Recorder's online search lets you view and print document images at no charge. A deed copy proves ownership but shows nothing about liens, so use a title search for that. In person or by mail, copies cost $0.50 a page.

faqs.q: Where do I send questions about my DuPage County tax bill?
faqs.a: Call the DuPage County Treasurer at 630-407-5900 for payments and the County Clerk at 630-407-5500 for tax calculation questions. Questions about the assessed value go to the township assessor listed on the bill. The Recorder's Office does not handle assessments.
